subject: Government
title: Citizenship, Human Rights, and Civic Duties
outline: Loss of citizenship: renunciation and deprivation
Rights of citizens and their limitations
Obligations of the state to its citizens

modules.title: Acquisition and Loss of Citizenship
modules.html:
1. Meaning

Citizenship is full legal membership of a state, carrying the entitlement to its protection and the obligation to obey its laws. A citizen enjoys full political rights (voting, holding office); an alien is a person residing in a state of which he is not a citizen.

2. Methods of Acquisition (Chapter III, 1999 Constitution)

MethodConstitutional basisExplanation
By births.25A person born in Nigeria before independence whose parent or grandparent belongs to an indigenous community; or born in Nigeria after independence with a Nigerian parent or grandparent; or born outside Nigeria to a Nigerian parent
By registrations.26A woman married to a Nigerian citizen, or a person of full age and capacity whose grandparent is a Nigerian citizen — subject to good character, clear intention to be domiciled, and the oath of allegiance
By naturalisations.27An adult of good character who has resided in Nigeria for at least fifteen years (including the twelve months immediately preceding), is acceptable to the local community, has made a useful contribution and intends to reside permanently

Other principles used worldwide: jus soli (right of the soil — place of birth) and jus sanguinis (right of blood — parentage). Nigeria mainly applies jus sanguinis.

3. Loss of Citizenship

  1. Renunciation (s.29) — voluntary declaration by an adult of full capacity.
  2. Deprivation (s.30) — for a naturalised or registered citizen who is disloyal, aids an enemy in war, or is sentenced to at least three years' imprisonment.
  3. Acquisition of the citizenship of another state, where the law requires renunciation.
  4. Conquest, cession or annexation of territory.

Dual citizenship: section 28 allows a Nigerian by birth to hold another citizenship, but a citizen by registration or naturalisation forfeits Nigerian citizenship if he acquires another.

examples.q: A Ghanaian woman marries a Nigerian man in Lagos. How may she become a Nigerian citizen?
examples.a: By registration under section 26(2)(a). As a woman married to a citizen of Nigeria she may apply to the President, satisfy him that she is of good character, show a clear intention to be domiciled in Nigeria, and take the oath of allegiance. She cannot become a citizen by birth, and she need not wait the fifteen years required for naturalisation.

examples.q: Can a naturalised Nigerian who takes American citizenship keep his Nigerian passport?
examples.a: No. Section 28 permits dual citizenship only for citizens by birth. A naturalised or registered citizen who voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country forfeits Nigerian citizenship. A Nigerian by birth in the same situation retains his citizenship.

modules.title: Rights, Duties and State Obligations
modules.html:
1. Rights of the Citizen

  • Civil rights: life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing, privacy, freedom of thought and religion, expression, peaceful assembly and association, movement, freedom from discrimination, and ownership of property.
  • Political rights: to vote and be voted for, to join a party, to hold public office, to criticise government, to petition.
  • Economic and social claims: education, health, work and welfare — in Nigeria stated as directive principles in Chapter II.

2. Duties of the Citizen

  1. Obedience to the constitution and all lawful authority.
  2. Prompt payment of taxes, rates and levies.
  3. Defence of the country and rendering national service.
  4. Respect for the rights and dignity of other citizens.
  5. Protection of public property and the environment.
  6. Voting at elections and participating in public affairs.
  7. Reporting crime and assisting law-enforcement agencies.
  8. Respect for national symbols: flag, anthem, pledge and coat of arms.

3. Obligations of the State

ObligationIllustration
Security of life and propertyPolice, armed forces, courts
Provision of social servicesSchools, hospitals, water, roads
Protection of rightsLegal Aid Council, National Human Rights Commission
Employment and economic opportunityJob creation, empowerment schemes
Diplomatic protection abroadConsular assistance to citizens overseas
Fair and equitable administrationFederal character, non-discrimination

Rights and duties are reciprocal: the citizen's right to security is matched by his duty to obey the law and pay tax; the state's right to obedience is matched by its duty to protect and provide.

examples.q: A trader refuses to pay tax, arguing that his street has no tarred road. Evaluate.
examples.a: His grievance is legitimate but his remedy is wrong. Payment of tax is a legal duty, not a conditional bargain; refusal exposes him to prosecution and reduces the revenue available for the very road he wants. The correct remedies are democratic and legal: petitioning the local council, pressing through market associations, using the Public Complaints Commission, and voting out non-performing officials.

examples.q: State two ways a citizen abroad benefits from citizenship.
examples.a: (i) Diplomatic and consular protection — the embassy may intervene where the citizen is detained or distressed; (ii) the right of return and residence in his own country, plus a passport as evidence of nationality, which no state may arbitrarily withdraw from a citizen by birth.

modules.title: Meaning of citizenship and nationality
modules.html:
Meaning of citizenship and nationality is a key part of Citizenship, Human Rights, and Civic Duties (SSS 2, Government). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • Meaning Citizenship is full legal membership of a state, carrying the entitlement to its protection and the obligation to obey its laws.
  • Loss of Citizenship Renunciation (s.29) — voluntary declaration by an adult of full capacity.
  • Acquisition of the citizenship of another state, where the law requires renunciation.
  • Dual citizenship: section 28 allows a Nigerian by birth to hold another citizenship, but a citizen by registration or naturalisation forfeits Nigerian citizenship if he acquires another.
  • Jus sanguinis means right of blood — citizenship follows descent.

Worked example

Q: Citizenship acquired because one's parent is a citizen illustrates:
A: Jus sanguinis — Jus sanguinis means right of blood — citizenship follows descent.

Q: Dual citizenship in Nigeria is permitted for citizens by:
A: Birth — Section 28 restricts dual citizenship to citizens by birth.

examples.q: Citizenship acquired because one's parent is a citizen illustrates:
examples.a: Jus sanguinis — Jus sanguinis means right of blood — citizenship follows descent.

examples.q: Dual citizenship in Nigeria is permitted for citizens by:
examples.a: Birth — Section 28 restricts dual citizenship to citizens by birth.

modules.html:

Key points

  • Meaning Citizenship is full legal membership of a state, carrying the entitlement to its protection and the obligation to obey its laws.
  • A citizen enjoys full political rights (voting, holding office); an alien is a person residing in a state of which he is not a citizen.
  • Loss of Citizenship Renunciation (s.29) — voluntary declaration by an adult of full capacity.
  • Acquisition of the citizenship of another state, where the law requires renunciation.
  • Dual citizenship: section 28 allows a Nigerian by birth to hold another citizenship, but a citizen by registration or naturalisation forfeits Nigerian citizenship if he acquires another.

Worked example

Q: Dual citizenship in Nigeria is permitted for citizens by:
A: Birth — Section 28 restricts dual citizenship to citizens by birth.

Q: A person residing in a state of which he is not a citizen is an:
A: Alien — Aliens enjoy protection of the law but lack full political rights.

examples.a: Birth — Section 28 restricts dual citizenship to citizens by birth.

examples.q: A person residing in a state of which he is not a citizen is an:

quiz.q: Citizenship acquired because one's parent is a citizen illustrates:
quiz.solution: Jus sanguinis means right of blood — citizenship follows descent.

quiz.q: Naturalisation in Nigeria requires residence of at least:
quiz.solution: Section 27 requires fifteen years' residence, including the twelve months immediately preceding the application.

quiz.q: Dual citizenship in Nigeria is permitted for citizens by:
quiz.solution: Section 28 restricts dual citizenship to citizens by birth.

quiz.q: A person residing in a state of which he is not a citizen is an:
quiz.solution: Aliens enjoy protection of the law but lack full political rights.

quiz.q: Which chapter of the 1999 Constitution deals with citizenship?
quiz.solution: Chapter III, sections 25–32, governs citizenship.

quiz.q: Voluntary giving up of citizenship is:
quiz.solution: Renunciation under section 29 is the citizen's own declaration.

quiz.q: Which is a duty rather than a right of the citizen?
quiz.solution: Taxation is an obligation owed to the state.

quiz.q: Deprivation of citizenship may apply to a person who is a citizen by:
quiz.solution: Section 30 permits deprivation only for registered or naturalised citizens, e.g. for disloyalty.

quiz.q: The right to vote and be voted for is a:
quiz.solution: Political rights concern participation in the choice and exercise of government power.

quiz.q: Consular assistance abroad is an obligation of the:
quiz.solution: A state protects its nationals abroad through its embassies and consulates.

quiz.q: A woman married to a Nigerian may acquire citizenship by:
quiz.solution: Section 26(2)(a) provides for registration of a woman married to a Nigerian citizen.

quiz.q: Rights and duties are said to be:
quiz.solution: Every right implies a corresponding duty on the citizen and the state.

quiz.q: Which state obligation is directly served by the police?
quiz.solution: Internal security is a core obligation performed through the police.

quiz.q: A citizen who exposes corruption is exercising the right to:
quiz.solution: Freedom of expression covers criticism of government and disclosure of wrongdoing.

quiz.q: Jus soli means citizenship by:
quiz.solution: Jus soli, the right of the soil, confers citizenship on those born within the territory.

quiz.q: National service under the NYSC illustrates the citizen's duty to:
quiz.solution: Rendering national service is a civic obligation encouraged by the constitution.

quiz.q: The process of depriving a person of their citizenship is known as _____.
quiz.solution: Denaturalization is the legal act of stripping a person of citizenship, usually for those who acquired it through naturalization.

quiz.q: Citizenship can be acquired by all EXCEPT:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2022). Correct answer: Conquest.

quiz.q: Citizenship can be acquired by:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2023). Correct answer: Birth, Registration, Naturalization.

quiz.q: The process of withdrawing a lawmaker from the legislature by their constituents is _____.
quiz.solution: Recall is a democratic procedure that allows voters to remove an elected official from office before their term expires.

quiz.q: The Nigerian Civil War started in:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2022). Correct answer: 1967.

quiz.q: The first Nigerian President to die in office was...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Umaru Musa Yar'Adua.

quiz.q: The right of citizens to vote and be voted for is:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2025). Correct answer: Franchise.

quiz.q: The Nigerian Civil War ended in:
quiz.solution: Past question (WAEC 2025). Correct answer: 1970.

quiz.q: How many members are in the Nigerian Senate?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: 109.

quiz.q: The supreme law-making body under the Babangida military regime was the?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Armed Forces Ruling Council (AFRC).

quiz.q: How many members are in the Nigerian House of Representatives?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: 360.

quiz.q: Which Nigerian leader was the first to serve as the Chairman of the African Union?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Olusegun Obasanjo.

quiz.q: Who was the first Nigerian to serve as the Commonwealth Secretary-General?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Emeka Anyaoku.

quiz.q: The administrative headquarters of the United Nations is located in _____.
quiz.solution: The UN headquarters is in New York City, USA, where the General Assembly and Security Council primarily meet.

quiz.q: The term of office for the Secretary-General of the Commonwealth is _____.
quiz.solution: The Commonwealth Secretary-General serves a four-year term and is eligible for re-election only once.

quiz.q: The primary aim of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) is _____.
quiz.solution: ECOWAS was established in 1975 primarily to promote cooperation and integration in economic, social, and cultural activity in West Africa.

quiz.q: Delegated legislation is made by _____.
quiz.solution: Delegated legislation (also known as subordinate legislation) is law made by an executive authority under powers given to them by an Act of the Legislature.

quiz.q: The African Union (AU) was established in 2002 to replace the _____.
quiz.solution: The AU replaced the Organization of African Unity (OAU) to better address the challenges of integration and development on the continent.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an obligation of a citizen?
quiz.solution: Citizens have duties or obligations to the state, such as paying taxes, obeying laws, and voting, which are different from their rights/claims.

quiz.q: The 'Oyo Mesi' were _____ in the pre-colonial Oyo Empire.
quiz.solution: The Oyo Mesi was a council of seven chiefs who acted as king-makers and provided checks on the Alaafin's power.

quiz.q: Universal Adult Suffrage means the right of _____.
quiz.solution: Suffrage refers to the right to vote. Universal adult suffrage ensures that all qualified adults can vote regardless of property or gender.

quiz.q: The main objective of the Commonwealth of Nations is _____.
options: to foster cooperation among former British colonies
quiz.solution: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of independent states, most of which were formerly under British rule, collaborating on social and economic goals.

quiz.q: A disadvantage of a one-party system is that it _____.
quiz.solution: Because there is no legal opposition, a one-party system often leads to the suppression of dissenting voices and the rise of authoritarianism.

quiz.q: In the pre-colonial Hausa/Fulani system, the head of a district was the _____.
quiz.solution: The Hakimi was the district head appointed by the Emir to oversee a specific area within the Emirate.

quiz.q: Non-alignment as a foreign policy means _____.
options: not taking sides in the Cold War between East and West
quiz.solution: The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was formed by countries that did not want to be formally aligned with either the USA-led or the Soviet-led blocs.

quiz.q: The primary purpose of the Civil Service Commission is to _____.
quiz.solution: The Commission is an independent body that ensures merit-based recruitment, promotion, and discipline of workers in the civil service.

quiz.q: Bicameralism refers to _____.
options: separation of powers between two organs
quiz.solution: Bicameralism is the practice of having two legislative or parliamentary chambers (e.g., the Senate and House of Representatives).

quiz.q: In the pre-colonial Igbo system, the 'Ofo' was a symbol of _____.
quiz.solution: The Ofo was a sacred staff representing the authority of the ancestors and the principle of truth and justice in Igbo traditional society.

quiz.q: A 'Confederation' is a system where _____.
options: component units are more powerful than the center
there is only one level of government
quiz.solution: In a confederation, independent states unite for common purposes but retain their individual sovereignty, making the central authority weak.

quiz.q: The headquarters of the African Union (AU) is in _____.
quiz.solution: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, is the capital of the AU, inherited from the OAU.

quiz.q: Gerrymandering is a term used in _____.
quiz.solution: Gerrymandering is the manipulation of electoral boundaries to favor one political party over another.

quiz.q: The first President of the OAU was _____.
quiz.solution: Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia served as the first chairperson of the OAU in 1963.

quiz.q: A bureaucratic organization is characterized by _____.
quiz.solution: Bureaucracy is defined by a clear hierarchy, division of labor, and adherence to formal rules and procedures.

quiz.q: The permanent members of the UN Security Council are _____.
quiz.solution: There are 5 permanent members and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.
